Bernoulli numbers and sum of powers of integers of higher order

Andrei K. Svinin Address: Andrei K. Svinin, Matrosov Institute for System Dynamics and Control Theory of Siberian Branch of Russian Academy of Sciences, P.O. Box 292, 664033 Irkutsk, Russia Email address: svinin@icc.ru and Svetlana V. Svinina Address: Svetlana V. Svinina, Matrosov Institute for System Dynamics and Control Theory of Siberian Branch of Russian Academy of Sciences, P.O. Box 292, 664033 Irkutsk, Russia Email address: gaidamak@icc.ru
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

We give an expression of polynomials for higher sums of powers of integers via the higher order Bernoulli numbers.

1. Introduction

As is known the sum of powers of integers [4], [9]

Sm​(n):=∑q=1nqmS_{m}(n):=\sum_{q=1}^{n}q^{m}

can be computed with the help of some appropriate polynomial S^m​(n)\hat{S}_{m}(n) for any m≥0m\geq 0. Exponential generating function for the sums Sm​(n)S_{m}(n) is given by

S⁡(n,t)=∑q=1neq​t=e(n+1)​t−etet−1.S(n,t)=\sum_{q=1}^{n}e^{qt}=\frac{e^{(n+1)t}-e^{t}}{e^{t}-1}. (1.1)

Expanding in series (1.1) yields an infinite set of polynomials {S^m​(n):m≥0}\{\hat{S}_{m}(n):m\geq 0\}, that is,

S⁡(n,t)=∑q≥0S^q​(n)​tqq!.S(n,t)=\sum_{q\geq 0}\hat{S}_{q}(n)\frac{t^{q}}{q!}.

It is a classical result that these polynomials can be expressed as [7]

S^m​(n)=1m+1​∑q=0m(−1)q​(m+1q)​Bq​nm+1−q,\hat{S}_{m}(n)=\frac{1}{m+1}\sum_{q=0}^{m}(-1)^{q}{m+1\choose q}B_{q}n^{m+1-q}, (1.2)

where BqB_{q} are the Bernoulli numbers that can be derived from the exponential generating function

tet−1=∑q≥0Bq​tqq!.\frac{t}{e^{t}-1}=\sum_{q\geq 0}B_{q}\frac{t^{q}}{q!}. (1.3)

It follows from (1.3) that the Bernoulli numbers satisfy the recurrence relation

∑q=0m(m+1q)​Bq=δ0,m.\sum_{q=0}^{m}{m+1\choose q}B_{q}=\delta_{0,m}. (1.4)

This relation is in fact the simplest one of many known recurrence relations involving the Bernoulli numbers (see, for example, [2] and references therein). One can derive, for example, an infinite number of recurrence relations of the form

∑q=0m(m+kq)​S​(m+k−q,k)​Bq=m+kk​S​(m+k−1,k−1),∀k≥1.\sum_{q=0}^{m}{m+k\choose q}S(m+k-q,k)B_{q}=\frac{m+k}{k}S(m+k-1,k-1),\;\;\forall k\geq 1. (1.5)

In this paper we investigate a class of sums that correspond to a kk-th power of generating function (1.1) for k≥1k\geq 1. Our main result is a formula for polynomials allowing to calculate these sums. It turns out that these polynomials are expressed via the higher Bernoulli numbers.

2. The power sums of higher order

Let us now consider a power of the generating function (1.1):

(S⁡(n,t))k:=∑q≥0Sq(k)​(n)​tqq!.\left(S(n,t)\right)^{k}:=\sum_{q\geq 0}S_{q}^{(k)}(n)\frac{t^{q}}{q!}.

We have

(S⁡(n,t))k=(∑q=1neq​t)k=∑q=kk​n(kq)n​eq​t.\left(S(n,t)\right)^{k}=\left(\sum_{q=1}^{n}e^{qt}\right)^{k}=\sum_{q=k}^{kn}{k\choose q}_{n}e^{qt}. (2.1)

The coefficients (kq)n{k\choose q}_{n} obviously generalizing the binomial coefficients originated from Abraham De Moivre and Leonard Euler works [10], [5] and extensively studied in the literature due to their applicability. From (2.1), we see that it is a generating function for the sums of the form

Sm(k)​(n):=∑q=0k⁡(n−1)(kq)n​(k+q)m.S_{m}^{(k)}(n):=\sum_{q=0}^{k(n-1)}{k\choose q}_{n}\left(k+q\right)^{m}. (2.2)

It is natural to call (2.2) the sums of powers of integers of higher order. Expanding

(e(n+1)​t−etet−1)k=∑q≥0S^q(k)​(n)​tqq!,\left(\frac{e^{(n+1)t}-e^{t}}{e^{t}-1}\right)^{k}=\sum_{q\geq 0}\hat{S}_{q}^{(k)}(n)\frac{t^{q}}{q!},

we get an infinite number of polynomials S^m(k)​(n)\hat{S}_{m}^{(k)}(n).

Our goal in the paper is to prove that

S^m(k)​(n)=1(m+kk)​∑q=0m(−1)q​(m+kq)​Bq(k)​S​(m+k−q,k)​nm+k−q,\hat{S}_{m}^{(k)}(n)=\frac{1}{{m+k\choose k}}\sum_{q=0}^{m}(-1)^{q}{m+k\choose q}B_{q}^{(k)}S(m+k-q,k)n^{m+k-q}, (2.3)

where Bq(k)B_{q}^{(k)} are the higher order Bernoulli numbers defined as

tk(et−1)k=∑q≥0Bq(k)​tqq!.\frac{t^{k}}{(e^{t}-1)^{k}}=\sum_{q\geq 0}B^{(k)}_{q}\frac{t^{q}}{q!}. (2.4)

The Bernoulli numbers of higher order appeared in [11] in connection with a theory of finite differences and then was investigated by many authors from different points of view (see, for example, [3]). These numbers are known to satisfy [11]

Bn(k+1)=k−nk​Bn(k)−n​Bn−1(k).B_{n}^{(k+1)}=\frac{k-n}{k}B_{n}^{(k)}-nB_{n-1}^{(k)}.

The number Bn(k)B^{(k)}_{n} with fixed n≥0n\geq 0 turns out to be some polynomial in kk. These kind of polynomials are known as Nörlund polynomials. One can find a number of these polynomials in [11]. For convenience, we have written out several Nörlund polynomials in the Appendix. The numbers S⁡(n,k)S(n,k) in (2.3) are the Stirling numbers of the second kind that satisfy recurrence relation

S⁡(n,k)=S⁡(n−1,k−1)+k​S​(n−1,k)S(n,k)=S(n-1,k-1)+kS(n-1,k) (2.5)

with appropriate boundary conditions [15], [4].

It is easy to prove that the higher order Bernoulli numbers satisfy the recurrence relation

∑q=0m(m+kq)​S​(m+k−q,k)​Bq(k)=δ0,m.\sum_{q=0}^{m}{m+k\choose q}S(m+k-q,k)B_{q}^{(k)}=\delta_{0,m}. (2.6)

The most general relation involving (1.4), (1.5) and (2.6) as particular cases is

∑q=0m(m+kq)​S​(m+k−q,k)​Bq(r)=(m+kk)(m+k−rk−r)​S​(m+k−r,k−r),∀k≥r.\sum_{q=0}^{m}{m+k\choose q}S(m+k-q,k)B_{q}^{(r)}=\frac{{m+k\choose k}}{{m+k-r\choose k-r}}S(m+k-r,k-r),\;\;\forall k\geq r. (2.7)

As is known S⁡(m+k,k)S(m+k,k), for any fixed m≥0m\geq 0, is expressed as a polynomial fm​(k)f_{m}(k) of degree 2​m2m, which satisfy the identity

fm​(k)−fm​(k−1)=k​fm−1​(k)f_{m}(k)-f_{m}(k-1)=kf_{m-1}(k)

following from the identity (2.5). Therefore we can replace S⁡(m+k−q,k)S(m+k-q,k) by fm−q​(k)f_{m-q}(k) in (2.3). In the literature the polynomials fm​(k)f_{m}(k) are known as the Stirling polynomials [6], [8]. These are known to be expressed via the Nörlund polynomials as (see, for example, [1])

fm​(k)=(m+km)​Bm(−k).f_{m}(k)={m+k\choose m}B_{m}^{(-k)}.

The following proposition also gives the relationship of the higher Bernoulli numbers with the Stirling numbers.

Proposition 2.1.

One has

Bm(k)=∑q=1ms⁡(q+k,k)(q+kk)​S​(m,q).B_{m}^{(k)}=\sum_{q=1}^{m}\frac{s(q+k,k)}{{q+k\choose k}}S(m,q). (2.8)

In (2.8), s⁡(n,k)s(n,k) stands for the Stirling numbers of the first kind [14].

It is evident that in the case k=1k=1, (2.8) becomes

Bm=∑q=1m(−1)q​q!q+1​S​(m,q),B_{m}=\sum_{q=1}^{m}(-1)^{q}\frac{q!}{q+1}S(m,q),

while in the case k=2k=2, it takes the following form:

Bm(2)=2​∑q=1m(−1)q​(q+1)!​Hq+1(q+1)​(q+2)​S​(m,q),B_{m}^{(2)}=2\sum_{q=1}^{m}(-1)^{q}\frac{(q+1)!H_{q+1}}{(q+1)(q+2)}S(m,q),

where HmH_{m} are harmonic number defined by Hm:=∑q=1m1/qH_{m}:=\sum_{q=1}^{m}1/q.

To prove (2.3), we need the following lemma:

Lemma 2.2.

By virtue of (2.7) we have

Rm(k,r)​(n)\displaystyle R_{m}^{(k,r)}(n) :⁣=\displaystyle:= ∑q=0m(−1)q​(m+kq)​S​(m+k−q,k)​S^q(r)​(n)\displaystyle\sum_{q=0}^{m}(-1)^{q}{m+k\choose q}S(m+k-q,k)\hat{S}_{q}^{(r)}(n) (2.9)
=\displaystyle= 1(kr)​∑j=0m(−1)j​(m+km+k−r−j)​S​(m+k−r−j,k−r)\displaystyle\frac{1}{{k\choose r}}\sum_{j=0}^{m}(-1)^{j}{m+k\choose m+k-r-j}S(m+k-r-j,k-r)
×S⁡(r+j,r)​nr+j,∀m≥0,k≥r.\displaystyle\times S(r+j,r)n^{r+j},\;\;\forall m\geq 0,\;\;k\geq r. (2.10)

It should be remarked that in the case k=rk=r, (2.10) becomes

Rm(k,k)​(n)=(−1)m​S​(m+k,k)​nm+k.R_{m}^{(k,k)}(n)=(-1)^{m}S(m+k,k)n^{m+k}. (2.11)

Proof of lemma 2.2. We can rewrite (2.9) as

Rm(k,r)​(n)=∑0≤j≤q≤maq​bq,j​nr+q−j,R_{m}^{(k,r)}(n)=\sum_{0\leq j\leq q\leq m}a_{q}b_{q,j}n^{r+q-j},

where

aq:=(m+kq)(r+qr)​S​(m+k−q,k)a_{q}:=\frac{{m+k\choose q}}{{r+q\choose r}}S(m+k-q,k)

and

bq,j:=(−1)q−j​(r+qj)​Bj(r)​S​(r+q−j,r).b_{q,j}:=(-1)^{q-j}{r+q\choose j}B_{j}^{(r)}S(r+q-j,r).

Let j~=q−j\tilde{j}=q-j and

bq,j~=(−1)j~​(r+qq−j~)​Bq−j~(r)​S​(r+j~,r).b_{q,\tilde{j}}=(-1)^{\tilde{j}}{r+q\choose q-\tilde{j}}B_{q-\tilde{j}}^{(r)}S(r+\tilde{j},r).

In what follows, for simplicity, let us write j~\tilde{j} without the tilde. Making use the identity

(r+qq−j)=(r+qr+j)=(qj)​(r+qr)(r+jr),{r+q\choose q-j}={r+q\choose r+j}={q\choose j}\frac{{r+q\choose r}}{{r+j\choose r}},

we get

aq​bq,j=(−1)j​S⁡(r+j,r)(r+jr)​(m+kq)​(qj)​S​(m+k−q,k)​Bq−j(r)a_{q}b_{q,j}=(-1)^{j}\frac{S(r+j,r)}{{r+j\choose r}}{m+k\choose q}{q\choose j}S(m+k-q,k)B_{q-j}^{(r)}

and therefore

Rm(k,r)​(n)\displaystyle R_{m}^{(k,r)}(n) =\displaystyle= ∑0≤j≤q≤maq​bq,j​nr+j\displaystyle\sum_{0\leq j\leq q\leq m}a_{q}b_{q,j}n^{r+j}
=\displaystyle= ∑0≤j≤m(−1)j​S⁡(r+j,r)(r+jr)​nr+j​∑j≤q≤m(m+kq)​(qj)​S​(m+k−q,k)​Bq−j(r).\displaystyle\sum_{0\leq j\leq m}(-1)^{j}\frac{S(r+j,r)}{{r+j\choose r}}n^{r+j}\sum_{j\leq q\leq m}{m+k\choose q}{q\choose j}S(m+k-q,k)B_{q-j}^{(r)}.

In turn, making use the identity

(m+kq)​(qj)=(m+kj)​(m+k−jq−j),{m+k\choose q}{q\choose j}={m+k\choose j}{m+k-j\choose q-j},

we get

Rm(k,r)​(n)\displaystyle R_{m}^{(k,r)}(n) =\displaystyle= ∑0≤j≤m(−1)j​S⁡(r+j,r)(r+jk)​(m+kj)​nr+j\displaystyle\sum_{0\leq j\leq m}(-1)^{j}\frac{S(r+j,r)}{{r+j\choose k}}{m+k\choose j}n^{r+j}
×∑j≤q≤m(m+k−jq−j)​S​(m+k−q,k)​Bq−j(r).\displaystyle\times\sum_{j\leq q\leq m}{m+k-j\choose q-j}S(m+k-q,k)B_{q-j}^{(r)}.

Finally, by virtue of (2.7), we get

∑j≤q≤m(m+k−jq−j)​S​(m+k−q,k)​Bq−j(r)\displaystyle\sum_{j\leq q\leq m}{m+k-j\choose q-j}S(m+k-q,k)B_{q-j}^{(r)}
=∑0≤q≤m−j(m+k−jq)​S​(m+k−j−q,k)​Bq(r)\displaystyle\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;=\sum_{0\leq q\leq m-j}{m+k-j\choose q}S(m+k-j-q,k)B_{q}^{(r)}
=(m+k−jk)(m+k−j−rk−r)​S​(m+k−j−r,k−r)\displaystyle\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;\;=\frac{{m+k-j\choose k}}{{m+k-j-r\choose k-r}}S(m+k-j-r,k-r)

and hence

Rm(k,r)​(n)\displaystyle R_{m}^{(k,r)}(n) =\displaystyle= ∑0≤j≤m(−1)j​(m+kj)(r+jr)​(m+k−jk)(m+k−j−rk−r)​S​(m+k−j−r,k−r)\displaystyle\sum_{0\leq j\leq m}(-1)^{j}\frac{{m+k\choose j}}{{r+j\choose r}}\frac{{m+k-j\choose k}}{{m+k-j-r\choose k-r}}S(m+k-j-r,k-r)
×S⁡(r+j,r)​nr+j\displaystyle\times S(r+j,r)n^{r+j}
=\displaystyle= 1(kr)​∑0≤j≤m(−1)j​(m+km+k−j−r)​S​(m+k−j−r,k−r).\displaystyle\frac{1}{{k\choose r}}\sum_{0\leq j\leq m}(-1)^{j}{m+k\choose m+k-j-r}S(m+k-j-r,k-r).
×S⁡(r+j,r)​nr+j\displaystyle\times S(r+j,r)n^{r+j}

Therefore the lemma is proved. □\Box

The recurrence relation, for example (2.11), uniquely determines an infinite set of polynomials {S^m(k)​(n):m≥0}\{\hat{S}_{m}^{(k)}(n):m\geq 0\}. We have written out some of them in the Appendix. For example, S^0(k)​(n)=nk\hat{S}_{0}^{(k)}(n)=n^{k}. On the other hand

S0(k)​(n):=∑q=0k⁡(n−1)(kq)n=(∑q=0n−1tq)k|t=1=nk.S_{0}^{(k)}(n):=\sum_{q=0}^{k(n-1)}{k\choose q}_{n}=\Biggl(\sum_{q=0}^{n-1}t^{q}\Biggr)^{k}\Bigl|_{t=1}=n^{k}.
Lemma 2.3.

The higher sums Sm(k)​(n)S_{m}^{(k)}(n) satisfy the same recurrence relations as in lemma 2.2, that is,

∑q=0m(−1)q​(m+kq)​S​(m+k−q,k)​Sq(r)​(n)\displaystyle\sum_{q=0}^{m}(-1)^{q}{m+k\choose q}S(m+k-q,k)S_{q}^{(r)}(n)
=1(kr)​∑j=0m(−1)j​(m+km+k−r−j)​S​(m+k−r−j,k−r)​S​(r+j,r)​nr+j.\displaystyle\;\;\;=\frac{1}{{k\choose r}}\sum_{j=0}^{m}(-1)^{j}{m+k\choose m+k-r-j}S(m+k-r-j,k-r)S(r+j,r)n^{r+j}. (2.12)

In the case k=r=1k=r=1, (2.12) becomes the well-known identity for the sums of powers [12].

Proof of lemma 2.3. This lemma is proved by using standard arguments. Let us replace an argument of generating function t→−tt\rightarrow-t to get

∑q≥0(−1)q​Sq(r)​(n)​tqq!=(−1)k​(e−n​t−1et−1)r.\sum_{q\geq 0}(-1)^{q}S^{(r)}_{q}(n)\frac{t^{q}}{q!}=(-1)^{k}\left(\frac{e^{-nt}-1}{e^{t}-1}\right)^{r}. (2.13)

Multiplying both sides of (2.13) by (et−1)k(e^{t}-1)^{k} and taking into account that

(et−1)k=k!​(∑q≥0S⁡(q,k)​tqq!),(e^{t}-1)^{k}=k!\left(\sum_{q\geq 0}S(q,k)\frac{t^{q}}{q!}\right),

we get (2.12). □\Box

Now, we are in a position to prove our theorem.

Theorem 2.4.

One has

Sm(k)​(n)=S^m(k)​(n),S_{m}^{(k)}(n)=\hat{S}_{m}^{(k)}(n),

where S^m(k)​(n)\hat{S}_{m}^{(k)}(n) be the polynomials (2.3).

Proof. This theorem is a simple consequence of lemma 2.2 and lemma 2.3 since the sums Sm(k)​(n){S}_{m}^{(k)}(n) satisfy the same recurrence relations as the polynomials S^m(k)​(n)\hat{S}_{m}^{(k)}(n). □\Box

3. The relationship of the sums Sm(k)​(n)S_{m}^{(k)}(n) to other sums

In [13] we considered sums of the form

𝒮m(k)​(n):=∑{λ}∈Bj,j​n(λ1m+(λ2−n)m+⋯+(λk−k​n+n)m),\mathcal{S}_{m}^{(k)}(n):=\sum_{\{\lambda\}\in B_{j,jn}}\left(\lambda_{1}^{m}+(\lambda_{2}-n)^{m}+\cdots+(\lambda_{k}-kn+n)^{m}\right), (3.1)

where it is supposed that mm is odd. Here Bk,k​n:={λq:1≤λ1≤⋯≤λk≤k​n}B_{k,kn}:=\{\lambda_{q}:1\leq\lambda_{1}\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_{k}\leq kn\}. Let us remark that there are some terms of the form rmr^{m} with negative rr in (3.1). It is evident that in this case rm=−|r|mr^{m}=-|r|^{m}. By this rule, the sum (3.1) can be rewritten as

𝒮m(k)​(n)=∑q=0k​ncq​(k,n)​qm\mathcal{S}_{m}^{(k)}(n)=\sum_{q=0}^{kn}c_{q}(k,n)q^{m} (3.2)

with some integer coefficients cr​(k,n)c_{r}(k,n).

It was conjectured in [13] that in the case of odd mm the sums 𝒮m(k)​(n)\mathcal{S}_{m}^{(k)}(n) and Sm(k)​(n)S_{m}^{(k)}(n) are related with each other by

𝒮m(k)​(n)=∑q=0k−1(k⁡(n+1)q)​Sm(k−q)​(n).\mathcal{S}_{m}^{(k)}(n)=\sum_{q=0}^{k-1}{k(n+1)\choose q}S_{m}^{(k-q)}(n). (3.3)

Let us define the sums 𝒮m(k)​(n)\mathcal{S}_{m}^{(k)}(n) with even mm by (3.2). It is evident that conjectural relation (3.3) is valid for both odd and even mm. More exactly, actual calculations show that

𝒮m(k)​(n)−∑q=0k−1(k⁡(n+1)q)​Sm(k−q)​(n)=c0​(k,n)​δm,0.\mathcal{S}_{m}^{(k)}(n)-\sum_{q=0}^{k-1}{k(n+1)\choose q}S_{m}^{(k-q)}(n)=c_{0}(k,n)\delta_{m,0}.
